Lucre
LOO-ker
n.
Latin lucrum, “gain, profit.” The KJV uses lucre almost exclusively in the disapproving phrase filthy lucre (aischrokerdēs in Greek), naming dishonest or unworthy gain.

Biblical Definition

Lucre in the KJV is almost always disapproving and almost always paired with filthy—filthy lucre—to render the Greek aischrokerdēs (literally shamefully-greedy) and its cousins. The phrase is most famously the qualification for church officers. Elders are to be not greedy of filthy lucre (1 Tim 3:3; 1 Tim 3:8 of deacons; Tit 1:7 of bishops); 1 Pet 5:2 charges elders to feed the flock not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind. The qualification is severe and structural. The minister’s motive in his service must not be money—not the salary, not the speaker’s honoraria, not the book royalties, not the platform’s profitability, not any form of pecuniary gain. Where the motive of money has entered the ministry, the office has been corrupted at its root, and the Spirit’s warning is sharp. Paul applies the same disapproval to false teachers generally: teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake (Tit 1:11)—the willingness to teach error for money is the marker of those who must be stopped. Beyond the disapproving register, lucre in older English could mean simply gain or profit in a neutral sense, but the KJV uses the word predominantly in the disapproving phrase, and the modern reader does well to hear it that way. Filthy lucre names not money itself (which is morally neutral as a means of exchange) but the love of money and the willingness to dishonor God or harm one’s neighbor for the sake of it. The love of money, Paul says, is the root of all evil (1 Tim 6:10); the love of filthy lucre is the same root showing itself specifically in the ministry, the office, the teaching that has been bought by it. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of a serious qualification for the office: men whose ministry is plainly not motivated by money, whose pattern of life shows them content with what they have, whose teaching is not for sale to the highest bidder—these are the men the New Testament calls to feed the flock of God, and the church saturated with such men is the church the apostles intended.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LUCRE as gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with the sense of something base or unworthy; in scripture, the disapproving phrase filthy lucre names dishonest or motivating-of-the-wrong-kind gain, especially in church office.

LUCRE, n. — Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with the sense of something base or unworthy. Not greedy of filthy lucre (1 Tim 3:3).

LUCRATIVE, a. — Profitable; gainful; producing profit or gain; as a lucrative trade.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 3:3 — "Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous."

Titus 1:7 — "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre."

Titus 1:11 — "Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake."

1 Peter 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind."

Modern Corruption

The doctrine of filthy lucre is corrupted by the prosperity-gospel and platform-evangelical traditions that have explicitly tied ministry to financial advancement and made teaching for money respectable—and by the inverse asceticism that treats money itself as evil, against Scripture’s distinction between money (neutral) and the love of money (the root of all evil).

expand to see more

The prosperity-gospel and certain platform-evangelical traditions have explicitly tied ministry to financial advancement, made the size of the offering a measure of the minister’s anointing, sold spiritual goods at premium prices, and produced a class of teachers whose pattern of life manifestly contradicts the apostolic qualification of not greedy of filthy lucre. The corruption is structural and pastoral: when ministry-as-profession is shaped by the same incentive structures as ministry-as-commerce, the apostolic Paul who refused even legitimate apostolic support (1 Cor 9:14-18) so that he might not be a burden looks like a strange figure, and Tit 1:11’s diagnosis (teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake) becomes uncomfortably contemporary. The recovery is the recovery of the qualification as a real test: men whose pattern of life shows them genuinely uninfluenced by money in their ministerial choices, whose teaching is not for sale, whose comforts are modest, whose financial dealings can be examined without scandal—these are the men the New Testament calls to the office.

The opposite corruption is the inverse asceticism that treats money itself as evil, refuses any compensation for ministerial work, and reads the New Testament’s warnings against filthy lucre as condemnations of money as such. Scripture refuses this. Paul explicitly affirms that the workman is worthy of his hire (1 Tim 5:18) and that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel (1 Cor 9:14); congregations are commanded to support their pastors and missionaries; the apostolic teaching distinguishes the use of money (legitimate) from the love of money (forbidden). The biblical balance is precise. Money is morally neutral; ministerial compensation is legitimate; filthy lucre is the love of gain that motivates ministerial choices, willing-to-teach-error-for-money, willing-to-sell-spiritual-goods-at-a-profit, willing-to-shape-message-for-financial-gain. Recover both ends. Refuse the prosperity-platform corruption that has made ministry-for-money respectable, and refuse the ascetic corruption that treats money itself as evil. The biblical pattern is content, honest, non-money-motivated ministers receiving appropriate support from their churches and free from the love of gain that the New Testament names as the structural disqualification for office.

Hebrew Roots

Latin lucrum (gain, profit); KJV’s filthy lucre renders Greek aischrokerdēs (shamefully-greedy)—the love of gain that disqualifies for church office and characterizes the false teachers whose mouths must be stopped.

expand to see more

Greek aischrokerdēs (G146) — greedy of base gain (1 Tim 3:3, 8; Tit 1:7).

Greek aischrokerdōs (G147) — for the sake of base gain (1 Pet 5:2).

Greek kerdos (G2771) — gain, profit (used both negatively and, in Phil 1:21, positively: “to die is gain”).

Latin lucrum — gain, profit (the etymology of lucre).

Usage

"Not greedy of filthy lucre—the apostolic qualification structural to the office of elder and deacon."

"Teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake—Tit 1:11 names the false-teacher pattern whose motivation is money."

"Prosperity-platform Christianity has made ministry-for-money respectable; ascetic over-correction treats money itself as evil; biblical doctrine distinguishes money (neutral) from the love of money (root of all evil)."
